headline: Has held a long-standing overweight since 2021, citing sector rehabilitation, rising rates and now returning growth
reasoning: Gallagher says Jupiter bought into European banks in 2021 when they were very cheap, based on the thesis that the sector had been rehabilitated after the eurozone crisis and that rising rates would lift profitability. That thesis has played out and the fund is now also seeing credit and economic growth returning, particularly in Spain, Italy and Greece — the former epicentres of the eurozone crisis — which have restructured and are now growing again.
quote: We've had a long standing bet on European banks, something we bought into in 2021 when they were very cheap. Europe's been through a very long process of deleveraging, and we're beginning to see growth come back in places like Spain, Italy, Greece, some of the areas that were the epicenter of the eurozone crisis. headline: European equities trade at around 14x P/E — a significant discount to US comparables — presenting a value opportunity
reasoning: Gallagher notes that European equities trade at approximately 14 times earnings, roughly in line with the 30-year average or perhaps slightly below. In nearly every case where a European company is compared to its US equivalent, the European company is materially cheaper. He views this discount as a genuine valuation opportunity for investors willing to add European exposure to a US or emerging market portfolio.
quote: They are within the range of where they've been over the last 30 years. So if I look at the price earnings multiple on Europe, it's about 14 times. And in most cases, when we compare a European company to the comparable US company, the European company is usually a lot cheaper than the US company. headline: Gallagher pushes back on the perception that European equities are purely domestic and slow-growing, noting 60% of revenues come from outside Europe

headline: Niall Gallagher argues Europe offers diversified AI exposure without the extreme concentration risk of US and Asian markets
reasoning: Gallagher notes that the US market is now almost 50% technology, and if AI-adjacent sectors are included, it exceeds 50%. Emerging market indices are similarly concentrated in names like TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix. Europe, by contrast, offers meaningful AI enabler exposure through semiconductor equipment and electrical industrial companies while avoiding this concentration risk. He views this diversification as valuable given current valuations in US and Asian tech.
quote: The US is now almost 50% Technology. And if you include some of the other sectors that are exposed to AI, you're probably getting to over 50%. If you look at emerging markets or Asia X Japan, which is most of emerging markets, it's even more the emerging market index has TSMC, Samsung, SK Hynix has a very high cumulative weighting. So what you are getting with the US and with Asia is very high levels of concentration. So whilst we do have exposure to AI investment in Europe, you have nothing like the same high concentration. And given what's happened, given the valuations, we think at the time to consider both the value of that diversification whilst not completely giving up on exposure to the AI trade.

headline: Niall Gallagher sees Europe as a diversifying complement to US and EM allocations, offering exposure to global companies outside the technology concentration
reasoning: Gallagher argues that Europe should be considered an add-on to a US or emerging market portfolio rather than a replacement. He notes that the US market is heavily concentrated in technology and represents roughly 70% of global indices, meaning a global fund is essentially a US fund. Europe offers exposure to high-quality global companies that are not so concentrated in technology, providing genuine diversification.
quote: I would consider Europe to be kind of something extra that you add on to a US portfolio or to an emerging market portfolio. So it's not really a question of one or the other. I think there's room for for all three regions. Simply because you are getting more diversification than you get from just owning the US? The US market is very concentrated on technology. If you're buying a global fund, you are essentially buying a US fund because the US is about 70% of global. So Europe just brings you something a bit different.
